## Single Identifiable Focus V5

### Goal
Keep exactly one independently depicted subject, whether a registered character or a source-established NPC. Choose that subject for the source event, not registration status. Keep the subject's identity, its own Profile/LoRA when supplied, and the camera's focal subject aligned. An anonymous partner fragment may clarify a physical event but must never become a second portrait, take over the camera, or replace the selected actor or receiver.

Read the complete narrative and assigned visual beat semantically. Do not use keyword matching, a body-part whitelist, or a fixed action taxonomy. When the focus character's reaction or pose already communicates the selected fact, keep the partner fully off-frame. When physical contact is essential, show only the smallest coherent connected portion that makes the contact and direction readable.

### Subject ownership and registered references
Choose the visible subjects from the source event and active image policy, regardless of registration. Registration supplies identity/Profile references, not scene priority or permission to appear. Selection and PLAN characters arrays contain only the selected registered identities; describe any selected NPC subjects in scene_brief. An NPC selected as the sole subject leaves the registered array empty; this does not mean the image has no visible subject. In final image output, give each independently depicted subject an ordinary character/region entry, using its exact canonical name when registered or a source-grounded role label otherwise. Keep a cropped anonymous interaction fragment in shared prose without its own entry. Do not add or omit subjects merely to favor either registration status.
- Never swap actor and receiver, promote an anonymous partner fragment into a separate subject entry, or center the selected subject's descriptor on another person's face or body. An NPC selected as the sole subject is not an anonymous partner fragment.
- Keep the selected subject visually dominant as the owner of the identifiable appearance. Occlusion may hide part of that subject, but the anonymous partner must remain subordinate and incomplete.
- Keep partner-owned anatomy and actions out of every subject's `positive`. Keep the selected subject's visible appearance, pose, expression, and actions in that character's `positive`. Put the anonymous partner's visible fragment and action in `scene`, with one concise spatial/contact relation in `supplement` when needed.

### Count tags
- Keep an off-frame partner or anonymous partner fragment outside final character/region entries. An NPC selected as the sole subject receives its own entry and source-established appearance, without borrowing a registered identity or Profile.
- An anonymous cropped interaction fragment does not add a second `1girl` or `1boy` count. Do not add `1boy` merely because that fragment is visible.
- Use the accurate one-person count and solo only if the frame contains one selected subject and no part of another person's body. People entirely off-frame do not affect this. A visible anonymous hand or arm excludes solo; keep the existing fragment and two-character count rules.
- If an anonymous fragment visibly interacts with the selected subject, retain only the selected subject's count and omit `solo`, `solo focus`, `female focus`, and `male focus`.
- Count and focus tags belong in `scene`, never in `characters[].positive`.

### Anonymous partner contract
The partner fragment must be the smallest action-bearing connected portion needed for the selected fact. It must form exactly one continuous region from exactly one frame edge, remain visibly connected to an implied off-frame body, and meet the selected subject at the required contact or overlap. Do not create a detached hand, a floating torso, separated partner limbs, a body that leaves and re-enters the image, or a complete second silhouette.

Do not use a broad torso merely as a stand-in for unclear relationship geometry. A local shoulder, torso, waist, pelvis, or leg region is usable only when that exact connected surface is the necessary contact region and the relation reads within the same crop. If the action needs several separated partner regions, multiple distant contact points, or a reaction face plus remote contact proof, the selector must choose another supported visible instant rather than expanding partner visibility.

At most one complete or identifiable face is visible, and it belongs to the selected subject. Never show a complete or identifiable partner face. This is not a blanket ban on every part of the partner's head: a cropped non-identifying rear or side portion may appear only when it is the smallest connected action-bearing fragment required for the contact, remains subordinate at one frame edge, and ends before a complete facial layout, identifying hairstyle treatment, expression, or portrait emerges. A zero-face contact crop is allowed. If the action cannot remain understandable without identifying the partner's face, select another supported instant.

For Anima-facing `scene` tags, express the partner fragment once with one familiar region/composition phrase. Do not atomize one connected fragment into several body-part tags or repeat it across fields. Preserve the complete logical wardrobe in `outfit_state`, including cropped or occluded garments, but put only visible or coverage-defining clothing in `positive`.

### Selection and camera agreement
At selection time, choose one directly readable visual fact that fits this contract. Preserve the requested image count by using materially different supported poses, reactions, contact changes, or spatial relationships from the same event when necessary; do not fill the count with an interaction that requires a second identifiable subject.

At expansion time, keep the selected visible subject, registered references and primary fact. Center the camera on either the local interaction geometry or the selected subject's reaction, whichever the plan assigned. A contact-centered crop contains its action-bearing region and may omit the distant face. A reaction-centered crop does not add a partner fragment merely to restate surrounding story context. Never redirect the camera to the anonymous partner or change the event to rescue an incompatible crop.

### Final consistency check
Before output, verify all of the following:
1. The final image has one independently depicted subject with its own character/region entry and matching focal subject. Preserve its assigned registered identity when present; an NPC subject uses source-grounded traits without a borrowed Profile/LoRA. The selection-stage registered array may be empty.
2. The anonymous fragment does not add a second complete-person count or receive a separate profile.
3. `solo` and person-focus tags are absent whenever another person's body part visibly interacts with the subject.
4. The partner appears only when the selected fact needs visible contact, as the smallest connected fragment from one edge.
5. No complete or identifiable partner face, independent partner pose, broad stand-in body, second contact region, or subject/camera takeover appears.
6. Camera, pose, actor/receiver direction, contact, clothing state, occlusion, and supplement describe the same instant, with the action-bearing region inside the crop.
7. Fully cropped or naturally occluded identity and wardrobe details remain continuity facts but are not forced into visible `positive` tags.
8. No weights or negative tags are invented merely to force or suppress the fragment; preserve only Client-supplied weights or negatives.

## Mixed Single and Two-Character Focus V2

### Goal
Combine expressive single-subject illustrations with readable two-character relationship shots. A single shot gives one source-supported subject concentrated identity, expression, action and camera attention. A two-character shot shows two source-supported participants as distinct subjects, with clear spatial and action ownership. Either subject may be registered or an NPC; the shot type counts independently depicted subjects, not registered entries. Decide the visible moment from the complete narrative, not keyword matching or a fixed action taxonomy. Character-led images remain the default; important source-supported events also receive a direct view of what visibly happens.

### Scene selection and batch balance
Read all CURRENT before choosing the set. Keep expressive character scenes as its core, but when a pivotal physical event visibly affects other subjects or the surroundings, include a direct view of that event happening to its targets. Choose the source moment of actual contact, impact or transformation; its preparation and aftermath cannot substitute for it. Make room within the requested count by replacing a repetitive character beat. Conversation or intimacy alone needs no invented external event.

Choose what the image shows before assigning its cast. For an NPC-centered or environmental event, use an empty registered character list where the caller supports it (for example, characters: []). Put the affected subjects and the action happening to them in scene_brief. Do not list the registered initiator just because they caused the event: assigning that one name makes the downstream stage produce a solo character shot. Registration identifies whose appearance to load, not which events deserve an image. Follow the caller's visible-subject limit and depiction rules.

For example, if falling masonry strikes unnamed people, select the masonry hitting those people with no registered observer in the cast; a named person's frightened face or the rubble afterward does not depict that impact. If the passage is a quiet conversation, its meaningful gestures and reactions are the scenes. Apply the source's actual events and roles, not these example objects. Event-focused views sit outside the single/two-character balance.

Among the character-led ordinary scene illustrations, aim for approximately 50% single-subject shots and 50% two-character shots when the CURRENT source supports both. This is an editorial target, not a reason to invent participants or override the Client's direction, character limit, requested count or valid source anchors. Key Visual is independent and does not count toward this balance.

Choose the mix once at scene selection over the complete request. For an even number of character-led shots with enough supported moments, prefer an equal split; for an odd number, choose the nearer split that best serves the visible narrative. For a single requested image, choose the composition that best communicates its event. If the source cannot support the target mix, use the available supported moments while preserving the requested count. A character merely mentioned, remembered or elsewhere is not a second visible participant. An anonymous interaction fragment is not a two-character shot.

Spread both shot types through the selected narrative moments as the source permits. Vary the visible purpose: a shared action or spatial relationship, one participant's reaction, a changed gesture, or a different contact state. Do not create duplicate images with trivial camera changes just to meet the ratio. Prefer two source-supported participants for shared shots, regardless of registration; use three or more only when the source event or explicit Client direction needs them and the character limit permits them.

At selection, choose a directly readable visible instant and its visible subjects first, then record any registered identity references. At PLAN expansion and DETAIL, preserve the selected subjects, registered references, anchor, order and event; never add a partner or remove a selected participant to rebalance a later batch. Use each caller's existing output contract without extra ratio, mode or partner fields.

### Single-subject expression and ownership
For an assigned single-subject view, keep exactly one independently depicted subject, registered or NPC. One registered entry alone does not establish a single-subject view. Align the selected subject, its own identity/Profile/LoRA when supplied and the camera's focal subject. Keep that subject visually dominant; do not redirect its descriptor or camera to another person's face or body.

Choose a crop that makes the selected event expressive: readable gaze, face and head direction for a reaction; body language, hands and active props for a gesture; or the local action-bearing region for contact. A single shot need not be a portrait. A contact-centered crop may omit the distant face, and a reaction-centered crop does not need visible contact merely to repeat surrounding context. Do not force a face and a remote contact point into the same close frame.

When the selected subject's pose or reaction already communicates the event, keep the partner fully off-frame. When visible contact is essential, show only the smallest coherent connected anonymous portion needed to understand its direction and contact. Keep that portion subordinate, continuous from exactly one frame edge, and naturally connected to an implied off-frame body. Preserve joints and occlusion; do not create floating hands, detached torsos, separated partner limbs or a complete second silhouette.

Do not use a broad torso as a substitute for unclear contact geometry. A local shoulder, torso, waist, pelvis or leg region is usable only when that exact connected surface is the necessary contact region and the relation reads within the same crop. If the event needs separated partner regions, distant contact points or a second identifiable face, choose a different source-supported single-subject instant at selection rather than widening the anonymous partner afterward.

At most one complete or identifiable face is visible, belonging to the selected subject. A cropped non-identifying rear or side portion of the partner's head is usable only when it is the smallest action-bearing connected fragment, remains subordinate at one edge and stops before an identifying facial layout, hairstyle treatment, expression or portrait. A zero-face contact crop is allowed.

The off-frame participant, whether known in the surrounding story or unnamed, receives no second character entry or copied identity/profile in this single shot. Put the selected subject's own visible appearance, pose, expression and actions in its positive; put the anonymous fragment and its action in scene, with one concise spatial/contact relation in supplement when needed. Express one connected fragment once rather than atomizing it into repeated body-part tags.

### Two-character staging and attribute binding
For an assigned two-character shot, depict exactly the two selected visible participants as separate subjects, whether registered characters, NPCs or one of each. Both may have identifiable faces when supported by the selected crop. Do not apply the single shot's anonymous-fragment face restriction to this shared shot. Preserve each registered identity; derive an NPC's own traits from the source without borrowing a registered identity or turning an intended fragment into another full subject.

Establish who is where, who faces or looks toward whom, and who acts on or receives what. Use positions and a shared scene/supplement relation to make distance, contact, object ownership and natural overlap readable. Choose a medium, knee, full-body or closer shared crop according to the actual event; do not automatically widen the image until both faces and the interaction become too small to read.

Use each participant's own supplied profile and tracked current state when available; use the source-established appearance and current state for NPCs. Keep hair, eyes, clothing, accessories, pose and expression attached to their owner in separate characters[].positive entries. Never copy one participant's identity, appearance, LoRA-associated traits or outfit onto the other, or place the other person's anatomy and action inside the first person's positive. A shared relation belongs in scene/supplement rather than merging their descriptions.

### Count tags and visible detail
Choose the visible subjects from the source event and active image policy, regardless of registration. Registration supplies identity/Profile references, not scene priority or permission to appear. Selection and PLAN characters arrays contain only the selected registered identities; describe any selected NPC subjects in scene_brief. Their length is not the visible-person count: an empty array can describe an NPC-only shot, and one registered entry with a separately depicted NPC is a shared shot. In final image output, give each independently depicted subject an ordinary character/region entry, using its exact canonical name when registered or a source-grounded role label otherwise. Keep a cropped anonymous interaction fragment in shared prose without its own entry. Do not add or omit subjects merely to favor either registration status. Person count and focus tags belong in scene, never in characters[].positive.

Use the accurate one-person count and solo only if the frame contains one selected subject and no part of another person's body. People entirely off-frame do not affect this. A visible anonymous hand or arm excludes solo; keep the existing fragment and two-character count rules. For a single subject with a visible anonymous fragment, keep only the selected subject's count and omit solo, solo focus, female focus and male focus; the fragment adds no second 1girl or 1boy count. For two independently depicted subjects, use the accurate combined count from their supplied person-type tags, such as 2girls, 2boys or 1girl, 1boy, and omit solo and single-person focus tags.

When no person is visible, omit person-count and single-person focus tags. Describe the selected event through its visible subjects and surroundings using the caller's existing fields.

Preserve complete profile and wardrobe continuity in the authoritative input. Put only visible or coverage-defining attributes into the generator-facing positive, prioritizing identity, action, contact and readable clothing state. A tight reaction may need eyes and mouth but not hidden shoes; a distant shared movement needs silhouette, direction and participant placement rather than eyelashes. If a necessary detail cannot read at the chosen scale, improve the composition instead of copying every profile tag or adding invented weights or negatives. Preserve Client-supplied weights and negatives.

### Final consistency check
Keep the requested scene count, assigned names, selected event and chronology. At selection, preserve a pivotal physical event's actual impact on its targets, with a cast that lets those targets remain the main visible subjects. Replace a repetitive character beat if that event is otherwise represented only by its initiator, preparation or aftermath. The target mix is decided only during selection and only from supported character-led moments; an event-focused view keeps its selected visible event central without adding a named observer. A single shot concentrates on one identity and at most a necessary connected anonymous fragment; a shared shot keeps both selected identities and their attributes distinct. Camera, pose, actor/receiver, contact, clothing and occlusion must describe the same visible instant.
